summary:
AETHER is an interactive Martian exploration and EVA planning platform that aims to support future astronauts to safely explore Mars and make informed decisions on surface missions.

Mars is extremely difficult to explore with humans, with challenging topography, low oxygen, shifting environmental conditions and many hours of communication delay with the planet. The risks are being mitigated in AETHER through integrating the functions of route planning, terrain visualization and mission safety checks within a single interactive interface.

Users can view locations on Mars, plan multi-stop routes, calculate distances and times, and analyze potential hazards, infrared layers, daylight availability, mission conditions, and more. A very important feature is the mission safety assessment system, which provides a clear warning of whether the mission can or cannot be safely flown, and highlights potential hazards, like lack of emergency return time.

AETHER is a proof-of-concept that illustrates how planetary mapping and astronaut safety planning can be used together to enable human exploration on Mars.AETHER is a proof-of-concept to show the potential for planetary mapping and astronaut safety planning to collaborate in enabling human exploration on Mars.
details:
Project Overview

AETHER is an interactive Mars exploration and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) planning tool which revolves around a single question: Can astronauts accomplish their mission and return safely?

Exploring Mars is fraught with difficult terrain, low oxygen, variable environmental conditions and communications delays to Earth. When something goes wrong, astronauts are unable to have immediate help. AETHER solves this by combining navigation, awareness of the environment and mission safety planning into a single application.

interactive system.

How AETHER Works

Our platform emphasizes the Gale Crater and Mount Sharp on Mars, giving users a chance to explore the Martian surface, and to plan scientific missions with multiple stops.

Key features include:

  • Interactive Martian Mapping: View terrain with map, photos and 3D visualization and use the helmet-view interface.
  • Smart Route Planning: Make multiple plans and display the distances, travel times and mission schedules.
  • GO/NO-GO Safety Assessment: Assesses mission conditions with regards to route safety; spacesuit limitations; daylight; rescue access; communications; terrain; weather; and solar conditions.
  • Emergency Return Planning: Determine when astronauts might be too far from safety and when they might not have enough emergency oxygen to return.
  • Terrain and Thermal Layers: View slope hazards, infrared information (during the day and night), and the path Curiosity will travel.
  • Mission Alerts: Show clear warning messages for certain missions/routes that may be dangerous.

In our example, the estimated return time is beyond the emergency oxygen time at the route's end, so the route is marked NO-GO in our prototype. AETHER does not just show a route, it provides an explanation of the safety issue and reminds the crew to rethink their plan.

Creativity and Innovation

The difference between AETHER and a normal planetary map is that it is not a navigation-only map, but a map for mission decisions.

AETHER combines environmental measurements, safety information and interpretations of separate maps.

With interactive hazard layers, multi-stop exploration routes, and understandable, GO/NO-GO hazard assessments, the complex mission information presented here is easier to understand.

Our design uses the publicly available resources available from NASA in the field of Mars exploration and planetary mapping, specifically terrain visualization and rover exploration around Mount Sharp.

Development and Technical Approach

The software prototype that is being developed is an interactive software prototype, which runs in a browser. It's interface features layered planetary mapping, route-planning options, safety-status panels, and multiple visualization modes.

It is built around a mock astronaut exploration process, from target selection to reviewing environmental data, and before an EVA commences to evaluate risk.

This is a current prototype of the planning concept, not a flight certified navigation or life support system.

Factors Considered

Our team developed during the design process the astronaut safety concerns, the risk message needs to be understandable, terrain accessibility, travel time, emergency oxygen availability, daylight availability, and the time lag between Mars and Earth communication.

How astronauts in spacesuits could interpret mission information quickly without having to navigate through complicated scientific data in a time critical situation was also taken into account.

Intended Impact and Future Vision

AETHER will show how NASA's knowledge gained in Mars exploration can be used to assist in the conduct of safer, more informed human surface missions to Mars.

The platform will be extended in the future with validated environmental models, more advanced hazard analysis, locally available mission data, and further advanced navigation assistance.

With human exploration coming closer to the planet Mars, it will not be enough to know where to go. Astronauts will also have to be aware of the dangers they face on the way to Mars and if they are able to make it back.

And AETHER is founded on that principle: Explore farther. Decide smarter. Return safely.
